ending1.title: The Steward Dismissed
ending1.subtitle: The Secretariat does not judge you. The Secretariat handles dates
ending1.text:
The letter came on the first of November. The Secretariat seal.

The temporary residence and labour guarantee numbered VS-18-0947 expired on the thirtieth of October. No renewal was submitted by the guarantor. Under Chapter Fourteen of the Basic Law, the holder is required to depart the territory of the Kingdom of Marigni within seven days of expiry.

With National Day close, the Secretariat sends its customary greetings to all residents.

Below that, in small type: this letter does not constitute an assessment of the holder’s performance of service.

You read the letter twice. The second time you read the small type.

Packing took half a morning.

You came with one case and you leave with one case. The general ledger for the month stays on the desk. It is not yours.

The pale rectangle on the right-hand side of the desk is still there. You never did work out what used to stand on it.

Martha made up a parcel of food for you. Handing it over she said “for the road”, and then turned back into the kitchen, walking faster than she usually walks.

Elena is not there. All morning she is not where she ought to be.

Nobody told Gregor to take you, but he brought the cart round.

It is forty minutes from the estate to Valehold North. You go by the road you came in on, except that this time there is nothing on the maples. The leaves all came down in last week’s frost, and the two rows of branches are bare, and you can see the sky.

A month ago this road was burning.

The groom does not say one word.

At the platform the flag under the eaves is tugged at by the wind. Gregor lifts the case down and sets it on the steps, the same movement as a month ago, only in the other direction.

variants.stable_repaired:
{@gregor}“The roof will not leak this year.”

Then he leads the horse away.
variants.plain:
{@gregor}“Mind the road.”

Then he leads the horse away.
variants.henk:
The west store room was locked while you were packing.

You take nothing out of it. None of it was yours, and none of it ever was.

You left a note for the next steward, setting it out plainly where the goods that are not in the books had come from, when they came, and how much of it there was.

You looked at it a long time after you had written it, and then you tore it up.

The next one will find it out.

Or will not.
variants.early:
The Baron’s man came in the morning.

Not a letter from the Secretariat. The Secretariat handles dates, and this did not wait for a date.

What he brought was the Baron’s own hand, half a sheet, written quickly.

“Payment stops today. Hand over within three days.”

Maplegate settled not one account this month. The day-labourers’ wages, the smith’s bill, the flour cart that comes every week — all of them blank in your ledger.

A thing like that travels faster than other things. By the time the note arrived, three houses in Valehold had already stopped giving Maplegate credit.

The tenants made no trouble. They simply stopped coming. In those last days there were fewer of them in the fields each day, and standing on the bank in the morning what you saw was wheat with nobody cutting it.

The handover took three days. Elena laid out every document for the man who came, not one of them missing, done more carefully than she did it while you were here.

The man who came asked her where the month’s record of expenditure was, and she said there had been none.

On the morning you left, Martha cooked as she always does, half an hour earlier than usual. She put a parcel on the table and went back into the kitchen.

Nobody told Gregor to take you, but he brought the cart round.

It is forty minutes from the estate to Valehold North. The wheat is still in the fields, and the two rows of maples have not dropped their leaves. This autumn is only half over.

He does not say one word.

At the platform he lifts the case down and sets it on the steps.
variants.early_subtitle: It did not wait for the term

ending2.title: The Competent Outsider
ending2.subtitle: You stayed, and what told you so was a letter
ending2.text: The Baron’s letter came on the thirty-first of October.

variants.lord_warm:
The renewal was signed on the twenty-ninth of October and is enclosed. Submit it to the Secretariat within seven days.

I have seen the harvest figures. For one month, properly handled.

von Alder
variants.lord_plain:
The renewal was signed on the twenty-ninth of October and is enclosed. Submit it to the Secretariat within seven days.

Have a fair copy of this quarter’s general ledger and of the tenant roll sent in with the renewal.

von Alder
variants.tail:
And so you stayed.

You put the letter on the desk with the renewal underneath it. There is a blank on it, in the same place as on the guarantee thirty days ago, waiting for your name.

You signed the same name.

Sitting in the office, you hear the kitchen below. Today is no different from yesterday, and tomorrow will be no different from today.

You stayed, and what told you so was a letter.
variants.henk:
On the day the renewal came through you went out to the west store room.

It is all still there. You counted it over: grain, timber, that cloth sack. The same as the night it was loaded.

You locked the door.

You stayed. Part of the reason for that has been left in this room, and the key to this room now hangs at your belt.

ending3.title: One of the Valley
ending3.subtitle: Nobody announced anything. Nobody read out any terms
ending3.text: The letter came on the thirty-first of October, and this time it is in the Baron’s own hand.

variants.letter:
The renewal was signed on the twenty-ninth of October and is enclosed. Submit it to the Secretariat within seven days.

I have seen the harvest figures. For one month, properly handled.

von Alder
variants.marguerite_line: Appended: the Baroness at Thornwall wrote and mentioned you. She very seldom mentions anybody.
variants.feast:
The Kindling falls in the last week of November.

For the three days before it nobody on the estate does any proper work. Martha fills the kitchen; the women from the tenant households all come, and from morning to night they are pickling and rendering and putting things down into jars. Elena washes every window in the main house, the high ones included, which are washed once a year. Gregor hangs a bundle of dry branches over the stable door and does not explain what it is for; you learn later that it is the custom here.

Master Lorenz brings the wood for the new fire. Branches down off that old oak at the hunting ground.

The fire in the forge-chapel has to be put out once on the night before, and then lit again with the new wood. It is the one time in the year the hearth is allowed to go cold.

You watch him do it. He presses out the last of the coals, tests the heat of the hearth with the back of his hand, and starts laying the new wood.

{@lorenz}“Only this one night every year,” he says. “And it must not be cold for long afterwards.”

You stand beside him and keep the draught off while he lights it.

At midday on the day itself the estate’s long table is set out in the courtyard.

Twenty-odd tenant households come. Old Wendt brings his grandson, and the boy keeps looking over towards the stable. Martha’s dishes come out from midday until dark, and not one of them is of a kind you ever saw in Forgehold.

You are seated in the middle of the table. The head is empty. That is the Baron’s place, and he does not arrive until the afternoon.

Halfway through the meal you find that something has appeared in front of you.
variants.unadmitted:
A small dish of pickles, which last month, in the kitchen, you happened to say you liked.

Martha is at the other end of the table filling glasses, and her laugh carries over everybody else’s talking.

You finished the dish that was meant for you.

After dark people start to go. The tenant households leave one at a time, and they take their leave of you on the way out, and it is not the way people take leave of a steward. Old Wendt’s grandson runs over to ask whether he can come and help in the stable next spring, and his grandfather pulls him away.

Once the table is cleared the courtyard is empty, and you stand in the yard and look at the light over at the forge-chapel.

You have not yet worked out what happened today. You only stand there, and the day feels long, and you do not want it to end.
variants.admitted:
A small dish of something pickled, which last month, in the kitchen, you happened to say you liked.

Martha is at the other end of the table filling glasses, and her laugh carries over everybody else’s talking.

You think of the twenty-seventh of October, on that street in Valehold, and the one thing you said to two men who do not belong here either.

I want a standing of my own.

You did not know at the time exactly what that sentence meant. You meant the card with the plant pattern on it. You meant eight years. You meant a recommendation out of a local jurisdiction; the inspector read the terms out very clearly.

And now there is a dish of pickles in front of you.

Nobody announced anything. There were no terms. Martha simply remembered one thing you said, and today she put it in front of you.

You finished the dish.

After dark people start to go. The tenant households leave one at a time, and they take their leave of you on the way out, and it is not the way people take leave of a steward. Old Wendt’s grandson runs over to ask whether he can come and help in the stable next spring, and his grandfather pulls him away.

Once the table is cleared the courtyard is empty, and you stood in the yard a long time.

Eight years. You work it out: seven years and ten months left.

You do not know whether you can last that long, or whether you will be at this table this time next year.

But today somebody put a dish of pickles by for you, and that needs no document to prove it.
variants.henk:
After the table broke up, going back to the office, you passed the west store room.

It is all still in there. Grain, timber, and that cloth sack heavier than you expected.

You did not go in.

This time next year, or sooner, a man will come over from Millridge about some very small thing.

ending4a.title: A Body Not Yet Received by the Flame
ending4a.subtitle: A man spent seven weeks twelve kilometres from home
ending4a.text:
You gave Thierry what you had put together.

You had no proof to point a direction. What you had was only the reason the man went, and when.

You told the forester everything you had understood, and then said you could not work out where he was.

Thierry did not answer at once. Where the wind is broken in this wood, where there is water, which hollow someone had been into in summer — he held it in his head.

{@thierry}“Then the few I can think of, I shall have to walk,” he said. “One a day.”

He looked you over. “It is bad going.”

You said you would come.

He said nothing more. You went with him for three days.

The first was the easternmost, the one with the stone bottom: empty. The second was the shaded one in the middle: empty too.

The third, on the second of November, was the highest. The hollow he had been into once, in summer.

From there to Maplegate is under twelve kilometres in a straight line.

A man spent seven weeks twelve kilometres from home.

The last stretch had no path. Thierry went ahead cutting a way with his knife and you put your feet where his had been.

The hollow lay beneath a ridge of rock. The water came first: a small pit with stones set round its edge, made by hand. Then the wall. The ruin of a stone wall, half a roof, enough to keep the wind off. At its foot, signs of a fire made more than once.

Thierry stopped. After a moment he went down. You followed him.

You saw a man at the foot of the wall.

Thierry crouched and looked at the leg first. There was a wound on the outside of the calf. Not deep, but it had gone a long time.

{@thierry}“Middle of October, about,” he said. “That wet spell.”

You think of those days in the middle of October. You were reaping. The weather was bad. You had worked out how much it was going to cost you.

He had very little with him.

A coat, a knife, a tin cup. And a wooden box.

Thierry gave you the box. He said he had not opened it.

You did not open it there either. You put it in an inside pocket, carried it all the way back to the estate, and set it on the office desk.

It came to rest exactly on the pale rectangle.

All four edges square.

Then you opened it.

There were only two things inside.

A certificate from the Valehold Lyceum of Stewardship. Land management. Dated twelve years ago.

A photograph. Four people standing in front of the main door of Maplegate — the same few steps you stood on thirty days ago with your case in your hand. An old gentleman on the left. On the right a middle-aged man in a steward’s clothes. Between them two young ones, one in his twenties and one about ten.

On the back of the photograph was a single line in pencil, in the child’s hand, pressed hard into the paper.

Hartmann took nothing with him when he went. Except this.

variants.rites_open:
The community Master conducted the rite of the Returning at the local temple, and it was set for the third day after the former family steward was found.

Lorenz did this for a man who had not died on an estate.

“By the practice there is no difference: a Returning is a Returning,” he said. “Where a man stopped does not affect his return to the fire.”

More people came than you expected. People from the three estates, tenants, several out from Valehold. Timothy came as well, in uniform, standing in the last row. He does not know Hartmann’s family. He only dealt with him for three years.

Baron Ludwig stood at the very front, and Martha stood beside him. She did not cry the whole way through. Her face was held very tight.
variants.elena_present: Elena came, and stood at the outside of the crowd, as far from the hearth as it was possible to stand. She never once moved forward.
variants.rites_close:
The hearth was opened.

A wave of heat came out and struck your face, and that temperature is not the temperature of a fireplace. It is something else. In that instant you understood something nobody had explained to you in thirty days: why this country built everything it has on fire.

You stood among the crowd and waited with them.
variants.ludwig:
He arrived on the third of November. That week, everybody in the House of Lords ought to have been in Forgehold.

Ludwig did not have himself announced. You were in the office, heard movement below, and by the time you came down the true master of the estate was standing in the hall with his coat still on.

{@ludwig}“Where is it.”

You brought the box down and gave it to him.

He opened it, but he did not take the photograph out, as though he had always known what was in there.

The Baron closed the box, set it on the narrow table in the hall, put both hands flat on the lid and stood beside it a while.

{@ludwig}“Ninety-six.”

After a while he asked a few specific questions. Who found him. Whereabouts. On what day the rite was set. Whom to notify.

You answered each one, and he heard all of it out.

And then he said something you were not prepared for.

{@ludwig}“Hartmann did not talk much as a boy,” he said. “I am ten years older. He was running about here with his father while I, then, was at school in Forgehold and came home twice a year. Every time I came back, he was sitting on those steps by the door.”

He turned his head to the door. It stood open, and the steps were empty.

{@ludwig}“Afterwards I sent him to the Lyceum; the stewards’ children all want to go there. But I never asked him what he wanted to do.”

He took his hands off the box.

{@ludwig}“I thought it did not need asking.”
variants.festival_mirror:
The Kindling falls in the third week after the Returning.

The estate’s long table is set out in the courtyard. Returning or no Returning, the Kindling comes. Twenty-odd tenant households come, the same number as other years. You gather together, gather before the fire.

You sit in the middle of the table, and the Baron takes the head. There is one more place laid at the foot of the table, with nobody in it.

Halfway through the meal a dish appears in front of you. A dish of pickles, the thing you happened to say in the kitchen last month that you liked.

You ask Martha who it is for.

{@marta}“It is laid every year,” she says. “It is laid this year too.”

She turns away to fill glasses at the other end of the table.
variants.henk:
On the day of the Returning you stood in the crowd.

People came from all three estates. Henk himself did not come; from Millridge there came a steward.

After the rite Henk’s steward came over and said a few civil things. That the Baron sent his regards. That it had been a hard autumn. That neighbours ought to help one another.

While he was speaking you were thinking about what is in the west store room.
variants.henk_ledger:
You thought of the reference in the ledger: three letters and two digits, five times, every entry recorded exactly. The same reference appeared in a carriage contract from Millridge three years before.

Hartmann had not been without dealings with Millridge. He had only kept a copy of every one.

The man lying in that fire is lying there because he refused Henk.

And part of the reason you are standing here, able to hand the estate over, is that you did not.
variants.henk_noledger:
The man lying in that fire is lying there because he refused Henk.

And part of the reason you are standing here, able to hand the estate over, is that you did not.

ending4b.title: A Man Brought Back
ending4b.subtitle: What you waited for comes, and you are not the one who waited
ending4b.text:
When you spread what you had in front of Thierry, it did not take him long.

{@thierry}“The highest one,” he said. “Water, shade, and this grows there. The other two, it does not.”

He took two men up the same day, and you went with them.

The last stretch had no path. Thierry went ahead cutting a way with his knife and you put your feet where his had been. As the light went you reached the top of a ridge of rock, and below it there was a fire, a very small one.

A man sat at the foot of a wall with his back to the stone and a coat pulled up to his chin.

He was alive.

He looked up at you and did not speak or move.

A wound on the outside of the calf, not deep, but it had gone septic and the swelling reached the knee. Thierry crouched and looked at it and said he had been feverish for days.

A day or two later there would have been no saying.

You spent the night in the hollow. Thierry made a stretcher from two poles and a coat, and at first light you began to carry him down.

You reached the estate at dusk.

The former family steward of the estate was wasted past recognition. Carried in, his eyes were open. He looked at the ceiling of the hall, then at the men carrying him, then back at the ceiling.

He knew where he was.

Martha stood in the hall with both hands gripping her apron, and did not say a word. In all your days here it was the first time you had seen her lost for words.

Gregor went to Valehold for the doctor. Three hours there and back, half the usual time.

Hartmann lay in that bed a long while.

He slept through most of the first ten days. Elena nursed him.

Nobody arranged it. The first night she carried a chair into that room, and from then on the maid did the dressings, the washing, the feeding, the getting up in the night to see whether the fever had come back.

Nobody in the kitchen spoke of it.

One day you went past that room and the door was ajar. She was putting a fresh wet cloth on his forehead. Her hands were very light.

She looked up and saw you.

She did not lower her head the way she used to. She gave you a nod, and went on with what she was doing.

The wooden box was on him.

It fell out of the inside of his coat while they were carrying him back. Thierry picked it up and set it by the bed.

For the past seven weeks he had kept it on him.

variants.awake:
It was the middle of November before Hartmann could sit up and talk.

By then you had been on this estate six weeks. Your renewal had come through; the second term is ninety days.

You went to see him. He was sitting up with pillows behind him and a board across his knees, which Elena had found for him, so that he could have something to read.

There is nothing on the board.

{@hartmann}“So you are the new steward,” he said, looking at you.

His voice was weak, but clear. He spoke the way you had imagined he would. Exact.

You said you were.

{@hartmann}“I have already asked about the estate,” he said.

That stopped you for a moment.

{@hartmann}“Martha has sat here twice. Gregor came once, stood in the doorway and said three sentences.” He said: “Elena is here every day.”

He shifted the board on his knees.

{@hartmann}“The harvest figures, how much of the dues was paid, how many of those five households were repaired, how far the woodland boundary was looked into. I already know all of it.”

{@hartmann}“So I shall not ask you any of that.”

He paused.

{@hartmann}“And besides, how those things were handled has already made clear what sort of person you are.”

He offered no warm praise. It was only a man who had been the family steward for eight years stating something he was qualified to judge.

The room is quiet a while. Beyond the window, in the direction of Maplegate Avenue, the crowns of the trees are empty now.

{@hartmann}“So I shall ask you something else.”

Then he asked.

{@hartmann}“Why do you want to stay?”
variants.admitted:
You said it.

On the twenty-seventh of October, on that street in Valehold, you said it to two men who do not belong here either. One of them was posted here. The other earned his place.

But this time you said more of it than you did then.

Because on the street that day you meant the card, the one with the plant pattern on it, and eight years, and a recommendation out of a local jurisdiction. You thought at the time that was the thing you wanted.

This time you meant something else. You named a few very particular things. Added together they do not amount to a legal reason, but when you had finished you knew yourself that they were the reason.
variants.unadmitted:
What you said was not the contract and not the term. You could not get those out any more; they were true two months ago and they are not now — or not only that.

You named a few particular things. That place in the kitchen. The smell of the stable in the morning. The way nobody in the fields spoke on the day of the first hard frost. One afternoon you sat in the forge-chapel and thought about nothing at all.

It came out badly. When you had finished you felt you had answered nothing.

He did not press.
variants.after:
He heard you out, and looked out of the window.

{@hartmann}“Valewisp people have a saying,” he said. “That some things are come by through waiting.”

{@hartmann}“I believed it for thirty years.”

He put his hand on the empty board across his knees.

{@hartmann}“But they do not say the second half of it.”

{@hartmann}“What you waited for comes, but you are no longer the person who waited for it.”

The room is very quiet. Somebody is moving about downstairs. Elena, most likely.

{@hartmann}“Has Kessler told you the term of years?” he asked suddenly.

Eight years, and a recommendation out of a local jurisdiction. He had said so.

{@hartmann}“He is right. Those are the terms.”

He was quiet a moment.

{@hartmann}“But eight years is not only eight years. Eight years is how long it takes a person to become somebody else.”

{@hartmann}“It is your decision. But what you decide now, the person eight years from now is the one who has to make it good. And that person is not you.”

He is only stating something he has verified.
variants.continued:
After a while Hartmann changed the subject.

{@hartmann}“I have been away from here twice,” he said. “Four years at the Lyceum, in Valehold. The year I finished I went to Forgehold and stayed eleven months.”

{@hartmann}“Both times I came back.”

He looked at the window.

{@hartmann}“I have taken that train. Three tunnels, two passes, and coming out of the longest one the light floods in all at once.”

He paused.

{@hartmann}“But every time I took it, it was to come back. I do not know… what that road is like, when it is not for coming back.”

He turned his head.

{@hartmann}“You have travelled it.”

You told him about travelling that road.

You did not describe the colour of the south slopes, or the canopy turning from grey-green to gold. He knows those. He has lived in these woods thirty years.

You told him something else.

You said that before you boarded you turned round once on the platform. Across the River Forgel the upper town on the north bank showed only its outline in the morning fog: the spires of Crownblaze Palace, the dome of the Sanctum, and the stone span of the King’s Leap running together into one pale grey skyline.

You said what you thought then was: I never got over there to see it.

And then: perhaps I never will.

You said it was on that second thought that the carriage door closed.

He said nothing for a long time after that.

{@hartmann}“I lived in Forgehold eleven months,” he said. “I never once crossed the river to the north bank.”

{@hartmann}“Eleven months.”

He looked at his own hands.

{@hartmann}“I kept thinking there would be a great deal to do once I was back.”

Then he asked his second question.

And then his third.
variants.ludwig:
He arrived on the third of November. That week, everybody in the House of Lords ought to have been in Forgehold.

Ludwig went straight up to the room upstairs.

The door was shut, and stayed shut a long time. You were in the office below and heard nothing; the door of that room is thick, and neither of those two men ever spoke loudly.

You happened to be in the hall when he came down.

He stood at the foot of the stairs with one hand still on the rail.

{@ludwig}“He asked me what Forgehold is like.”

After a while he walked to the door. At the door he stopped and looked at those few steps outside.

{@ludwig}“Hartmann did not talk much as a boy,” he said. “I am ten years older. He was running about here with his father while I, then, was at school in Forgehold and came home twice a year. Every time I came back, he was sitting on those steps by the door.”

He pushed the door open and went out, and stood on the steps with his back to you.

{@ludwig}“Afterwards I sent him to the Lyceum; the stewards’ children all want to go there. But I never asked him what he wanted to do.”

The maples outside are bare.

{@ludwig}“There is still time.”
variants.henk:
That night you were in the office, reconciling. Where the goods in the west store room came from is not in the books.

You wrote a line on paper and struck it out.

The light in that room upstairs is still on. Elena is there.

The man in that bed is in it because he refused Henk.

And part of the reason you are still on this estate is that you did not.

You turned the page.
variants.festival_mirror:
At midday on the day of the Kindling the estate’s long table is set out in the courtyard.

Hartmann is not up to the table yet. Elena carried a plate of food upstairs.

You sit in the middle of the table. The head is empty; the Baron is upstairs. He said he would come down shortly.

He did not come down, after all.

Halfway through the meal a dish appears in front of you. A dish of pickles, the thing you happened to say last month in the kitchen that you liked.

Martha is at the other end of the table filling glasses.

After dark people go. Going up, you pass that room, and the door is ajar.

There are two plates on the table.

One is Ludwig’s, mostly eaten.

The other is on the stool by the bed, also mostly eaten.
variants.dawn_letter:
You wrote to the Baron that the man had been found. The reply came on the first of November, three lines long.

It said nothing of the harvest and nothing of the books. It asked one thing: where is he.

The renewal was enclosed beneath it, signed on the thirtieth of October, the last day of the term.

epilogue.title: Epilogue · Ludwig’s Three Days
epilogue.text:
Every year, at the Kindling, Baron Ludwig comes back and stays three days.

In those three days he does not go into town, and he calls on none of the neighbouring estates. Henk sends somebody with a message every year, and every year it is turned back.

variants.ending3: The Baron only arrives in the afternoon. He eats very little, but he stays in the courtyard until the end.
variants.ending4a: He looked at the accounts, and closed them after a few pages. Twice in the three days he went to the narrow table in the hall, where the box stands.
variants.ending4b: He went upstairs three times. The third time he stayed over an hour.
variants.close:
The Baron leaves on the afternoon of the third day.

The carriage waits at the estate gate. Before he gets in he does the thing he does every year: he stands a while at the entrance to Maplegate Avenue and looks at the two rows of trees.

It is the end of November. The trees are bare.

{@gregor}“The master stands there a while every year. It is something the earlier masters left behind.” He is unusually talkative.

“How long for?”

{@gregor}“Not long,” he says. “A minute. Two.”

Baron von Alder gets in. The carriage goes south down that tunnel until it cannot be seen.

And then the estate goes quiet.

Winter is not far off.
